lesson.title: Docstrings: Documentation Python Can Actually Read
lesson.summary: A docstring is a string literal placed as the first statement inside a function that describes what it does, and unlike a comment, Python stores it as a real, retrievable attribute on the function object.
lesson.body:
Function definition creates a named block of code, but a function's name alone rarely explains everything a caller needs to know. Multiline strings, written with triple quotes, are well suited to holding that kind of longer explanatory text, since they can span several lines without needing a continuation character on each one. A docstring combines both ideas: it is a multiline string placed as the very first statement inside a function body, and Python treats it specially.

The syntax is direct. Consider:

def area_of_circle(radius):
    """Return the area of a circle with the given radius."""
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

The triple-quoted string sits immediately after the def line, before any other statement, even for a description that fits on one line, which is the conventional style. Python does not just skip over this string as inert text; it attaches it to the function object under the attribute __doc__. Running print(area_of_circle.__doc__) displays exactly "Return the area of a circle with the given radius.", and calling help(area_of_circle) shows the same text alongside the function's signature.

Placement is not just a stylistic convention, it is a requirement: the docstring must be the very first statement inside the function body for Python to recognize and store it as __doc__. If even one line of ordinary code came before the triple-quoted string, Python would no longer treat it specially; it would just be an ordinary string that gets created and immediately thrown away, with no effect and no attachment to the function at all.

This is the key difference from a regular # comment. A comment is stripped out while Python reads the file and never exists once the program is running; there is no way to ask a function for its comments. A docstring, in contrast, is a genuine string object stored on the function itself, which is why editors, the built-in help() system, and documentation-generating tools can all retrieve it automatically, long after the source file was written. This attribute is not unique to functions a programmer writes either; built-in functions carry the same mechanism, so running print(len.__doc__) displays the documentation Python's own creators wrote for len, using the exact same __doc__ attribute. Docstrings are a single, consistent system used throughout the language, not a special convention invented just for user code.

For a function that needs more explanation than a single sentence, the docstring can span several lines: a short one-line summary first, then a blank line, then further detail about behavior, assumptions, or edge cases. Python only requires that the whole thing be one string literal; how much is written inside it is a matter of judgment based on how much a caller genuinely needs to know.

Writing a docstring for every function is not just a style preference, it is what makes a function usable without reading its implementation first. That practical goal, of documentation that actually helps a caller use a function correctly, is what the next chapter looks at more closely: not just the mechanics of writing a docstring, but what makes one actually good.
